method: AI editorial comparison of the 116 selected stems and their six displayed options. The 20 November school notice establishes the five assessed units. Individual class exposure, grade bands and eligibility retain their recorded dispositions. Grade labels attached to released questions on The Full Marks are editorial. Collins targets a grade range at book level. Neither source gives official grades to individual app questions.

benchmarks.I: June 2024 1H Q20 (Pearson examiner report) and November 2021 3H Q12. Common-base exponent equations and combining representations.
benchmarks.F: June 2017 2H Q10 (standard form baseline) and Collins Edexcel Achieve Grade 7–9 §1.4 Q2–3 (linked units, batch proportions and reversed quantities).
benchmarks.R: November 2020 1H Q17 and November 2021 1H Q11. Repeated subject and symbolic collection; for radicals, specimen 1H Q13.
benchmarks.G: November 2018 2H Q18 and November 2019 2H Q25. Infer equations from coordinates, intersect lines and use the resulting geometry.
benchmarks.S: November 2021 3H Q13. Translate related quantities into simultaneous equations and use their solution to recover a further quantity.

decisions.B: Grade 7+ target supported by editorial comparison of the problem-solving demand
decisions.R: Strengthen the mathematical reasoning or reduce opportunities to guess from the options
decisions.S: Additional technique needs coverage evidence or redesign
decisions.U: Indirect benchmark or mixed-topic / option shortcut needs closer calibration

rows.rationale: Prime-exponent divisibility for both squares and cubes is the decisive additional skill.
Combines comparison of exponential ratios with parity and a cube exclusion.
Must compare powers across two bounds and add only feasible C values.
Optimisation over simultaneous prime-exponent congruences exceeds the stated index-law evidence.
Distinguishing sixth powers from cubes depends on prime factorisation divisibility.
Converting to one linear constraint is relevant, but a very short product table can settle the maximum.
The two exponent constraints determine the inputs; the scaling then changes both exponents in a new expression. No offered answer supplies the inputs.
Simplifying the power quotient is only the first step; the student must compare the two scaling experiments and convert the exponent to a factor.
Uses coprimality and minimal positive integer solutions as well as signed-base reasoning.
A bounded integer equation and completeness of the pair list drive the sum.
Uses parity of a square exponent plus two inequalities.
Each substitution gives a different necessary exponent equation. Repeated first-condition-only and second-condition-only choices make both checks necessary.
Divisibility and square thresholds dominate after substituting only two n values.
The exponent factorisation is demanding but a tiny pair search and highly separated powers in the answers give a second easier route.
Compare powers of two with the six offered outputs; few feasible sums of exponents survive. Require an unknown coefficient or a second structural inference.
A common factor must be separated before taking the product and quotient; the resulting independent exponent equations determine the sum of squares.
Eliminating products of positive real powers is distinct from the school notice's basic index laws.
The linear system determines small exponents immediately and the rest is straightforward power arithmetic. Add a genuinely competing scaling condition.
Recognising a cube of the given monomial can solve the item by option inspection. Calibrate that recognition separately.
Translating the perfect squares to parity and bounding the ordered pair are additional prerequisites.
Optimising an integer product along a discrete linear constraint is a substantial extra method.
Reversing the ratio yields two distinct exponent equations and different magnitudes for the sum. The student has to account for both.
Rewriting the root and power quotient produces a linear exponent in n. Two observations determine its coefficients, including a nontrivial sign.
The admissible exponent differences and the restriction n<m determine the solution.
Establishing the primitive integer scaling direction and maximising it under two bounds drives the task.
Enumerating the few positive pairs may replace index reasoning. A closer released discrete-exponent comparator is needed.
Two inequality filters on simplified powers dominate the final sum.
Completing missing prime exponents modulo six is a separate number-theory demand.
Expanding shifted quadratic exponents is needed before the index comparison can be made.
Conservation of dissolved mass, concentration bounds and discrete dilution choices add separate prerequisites.
The demanding step is allocation of two compressed sizes. Compare as linear optimisation and group with 031, 032 and 040 for Mastery.
Complete option tuples disclose candidate loadings. Checking feasibility may remove the optimisation demanded in free response.

Like the Collins faulty-batch task, this requires recovering a count from mass and applying a percentage to that count. The item also imposes independent capacity and tare-mass limits; selecting a rounded box count alone gives a distractor.
The six prices constrain the purchase search. Compare minimum-cost reasoning as well as the powers-of-ten calculation.
A routine balance followed by quotient and remainder is enough. The answer pairs reveal the group count to try.

Combines the Collins-style change of scale and units with a second model for the output of two panel types. The provided area conversion removes a recall barrier; the split must still be inferred before converting back.
With only a few proposed shifts, one division for the time cap and one ceiling calculation decide the answer.
Main demand is the net change and the two limits on the number of steps. Standard form itself only changes the scale.
Rescale all quantities to millions and fit a straight line. Appropriate as applied linear modelling; standard-form Grade 7 demand alone is unproven.
Testing the supplied volume and pack tuples can replace constructing the particle balance. Require stronger evidence for MCQ demand.
The target follows from two consecutive rate calculations and a time conversion. Add reasoning about an unknown rate or competing schedules.
Distinguishing flush from sample and rounding the container count up are worthwhile but do not establish Grade 7+.
Subtract overhead, divide, then find the remainder. The minimum last load is only a check at the given values.
The key demand is a fixed-total allocation; classify with 003. The distractor below the minimum permits early elimination.
The change from a small to a large plot has a fixed marginal cost. Same optimisation structure as 003 and 031.
Transfer after two different losses is substantial ratio reasoning. The power of ten cancels throughout.
The marginal resource cost is the same underlying method as 031. Credit represents one allocation concept across these variants.
The fractional inverse is a strong released-paper match; the required integer count also depends on rational inequalities.
Substitution gives a square in x. Understanding a positive square root is central; a single numerical check eliminates several formula choices.
Calibration and the difference of two linear displays give a useful inverse, but the options reveal a repeated intercept.
The first known reading immediately gives the intercept. Testing y=37 distinguishes nearly all options without deriving the inverse.
The unwanted variable must be eliminated symbolically and two simultaneous reading changes combined with their signs. Three choices share the correct formula.
Replacing the unknown calibration coefficient gives a linear inverse. Most options can be excluded using only the second requested value.
Deriving the combined slope and intercept is worthwhile; numerical substitution may settle the paired options. Compare against an equivalent MCQ.
The invariant sum determines a coefficient, then the student has to use a different linear combination to invert the model. Knowing the coefficient alone leaves five choices.
After finding k, testing the simple inverse and one equality suffices. Several choices share the same formula.
Calibration of two affine expressions is direct and either numerical condition eliminates most choices.
Eight input values can be tabulated; the inverse is a one-step reversal after simplification.
Requires comparing rational inequalities and handling parameter domains and excluded values.
A short list of integers plus a one-step inverse can settle both parts.
The composition and fixed-offset condition are relevant, but nearly all proposed ordered answers fail a single numeric substitution.
Once composed, the slope directly gives the change. Extra wording does not add an independent deduction.
Comparing the two orders is useful but four options share the inverse and the rest is numerical evaluation.
The two compositions differ by constants, so the second output supplies an unusually short numerical route.
The square-root sign and coefficient matter, but x=4 occurs in only one offered choice and can be checked directly.
Two observations determine an affine law by differences. The one numerical test value alone selects an option.
Rational square roots, integer restriction and inequality bounds are additional demands.
Substituting the two small roots identifies the missing negative branch; no substantial inverse construction is needed.
The squared term has its minimum at zero; both roots then follow from a square of nine.
The two observations determine the straight line without finding either parameter. Five choices can be discarded by the requested numeric case.
Reversing nested affine operations yields a constant scaling factor directly.
A short enumeration settles the output-set part; inverse options are repeated.
A fixed calibration and a small finite scan permit direct testing without higher algebraic reasoning.
The combination of f(t) and f(−t) simplifies to one affine relation. The offered t values allow the numerical part to carry much of the discrimination.
Undo the displays in reverse order. The proposed numeric input can check both stages without deriving the symbolic component.
Choosing the negative root is important, but only one candidate gives the required input of −2.
Enumeration of perfect squares plus the simple inverse can remove most distractors. Compare as a mixed discrete-domain task.
Using the origin and two oblique vertices to compute area needs an additional geometry method.
An unknown gradient and an intercept bound jointly restrict integer k.
Equidistance and squared distances are required even after the line is located.
Two equations must be inferred from coordinates. Their intersection and both intercepts determine an exact triangular area, closely matching the released coordinate-geometry demand.
The original intersection fixes two derived lines. Finding the x-intercepts still requires reconstructing each line before comparing the results.
Derive two equations, find their meeting point, then use a second gradient to reach a new intersection. The answer choices supply neither intermediate point.
A percentage comparison and joint inequalities determine the interval after finding the two lines.
A reverse trapezium-area calculation gives the missing intercept. Ratio and area are at least as important as the line equation.
The vertical difference gives k in a single linear equation and the area follows from a direct trapezium formula.
Enumerating nine small inputs settles the question and no line needs to be constructed.
Intersect, reflect, then extend a parallel line. The reflection is an extra prerequisite and arithmetic is unusually simple.
Integer intersections depend on divisibility in addition to the ordering of two functions.
The stem explicitly permits a nine-row table; that route removes the inequality reasoning.
Derive the intercepts from the slope and their stated relationship, then recompute the second triangle after translation. A single area calculation is insufficient.
The area and sum constrain an integer factor pair and the gradient chooses its order.
Spread and ordering inequalities drive the solution; it can be completed without interpreting or constructing a line.
Use the separation of intercepts to recover the gradient, infer the third intercept via the midpoint, then intersect. Testing y=x−1 alone leaves three possible choices.
Find the first intersection and the parallel gradient, reconstruct a y-intercept, then use a different x-intercept to determine the final slope.
The ratio of intercepts supplies the gradient directly. Determining both the area and k is close to a graph benchmark, but almost all choices share k=1.
Equating gradient expressions determines k. A single numeric value alone rules out only two answers; a second gradient is needed, but the common denominator cancels early.
Internal division of a segment in a specified ratio and two distance-to-axis constraints add prerequisites.
Equidistance and a prescribed difference of squares of distances are decisive.
Requires using signed heights on opposite sides of an axis as well as a coordinate ratio.
Linear combinations of changes are substantial, but systems are supplied directly and ratios of differences are a distinct demand.
Joint divisibility of two parameterised systems and a multiple-of-four constraint are decisive.
Positive integer solutions, bounds and divisibility are required after eliminating the variables.
The price-difference system can be set up directly; the purchase combination and short prices need a closer MCQ demand comparison.
Adding the original pair and scaling a right-hand-side difference is enough. Five choices share the same ordered pair.
Only the change in one equation matters; the system for differences is shorter than solving both complete systems.
Divisor conditions and a non-multiple-of-three restriction control the final sum.
Two-stage mixture conservation and percentages are beyond bare simultaneous linear equations.
Subtracting the systems gives one short system for input changes. A signed fractional result does not itself establish Grade 7+.
Model two price lists, infer the count of each item from the change in bundle price, then reconstruct the original purchase. The offered amounts do not dictate the original unit prices.
The initial linear system is followed by discrete mass optimisation and packaging. Some options are eliminated just by the stated 16 kg cap.
Two hypothetical transfers generate distinct linear equations in the original quantities. A third transfer must be calculated from the common total.
Solving the constants first leaves a simple second linear system. Both systems are explicitly provided rather than constructed.
The given ratio fixes the first solution, but the coefficient inferred there must be retained for the modified system. Simple scaling by the changed total gives a distractor.
Positive-integrality testing of five named parameter pairs is a separate prerequisite and a finite shortcut.
The shared divisor of two right-hand-side differences governs the possible k values.
